[From Experiment 1, cited for: A priori power analysis and target sample size] We performed a priori power analysis using Cohen's method with the G*Power software (Faul et al., 2007).

[PAPER_0086, relevance_score=0.270] Results

We excluded trials slower than 1,500 ms or faster than 200 ms (eliminating 1.65% of total trials). We excluded scratch trials (1.90% of total trials) from all analyses, and error trials (1.43% of total trials) from the RT analyses. Table 4 displays the mean RTs and error rates. We analyzed performance on training and transfer items individually to assess our hypotheses.

[PAPER_0090, relevance_score=0.295] Transfer Items (Stroop Task)

We excluded 42 participants from the transfer analysis due to the absence of a positive ISPC effect for the training items. Subsequently, we analyzed the data from the remaining 68 participants.5 We ran a 2 (predictive cue PC: MC vs. MI) × 2 (trial type: congruent vs. incongruent) repeated-measures ANOVA.

[PAPER_0096, relevance_score=0.227] First Half-Transfer (Stroop) Items

Forty-seven participants were excluded due to the absence of a positive ISPC effect for the training items in the first half of the experiment, resulting in 63 usable participants. We observed the effect of trial type, F(1, 62) = 241.58, p < .001, ηp2 = .80, due to slower reaction times on incongruent trials (M = 658 ms) than congruent trials (M = 558 ms).

[PAPER_0151, relevance_score=0.326] Note that the participants who were analyzed in the first and the second halves of the experiment in Experiments 2 and 3 were not the same since we defined the inclusion criterion as having a positive ISPC effect with the training items in the corresponding half. Therefore, a repeated measures ANOVA would not be appropriate for comparing performance across the first and the second halves of the experiment since there would be missing cells in the comparison. Thus, we compared the performance across halves in Experiment 2 (and later Experiment 3) with a linear mixed effects model using subject as a random intercept.

items.paper_content_quotes:
[PAPER_0025, relevance_score=0.301] Transfer may occur in a near sense in which the learned control settings transfer to novel unbiased stimuli within the same task, or in a far (farther) sense in which they transfer to a novel task involving novel unbiased stimuli.

A few studies have examined the transfer of item-specific control settings in a near sense (i.e., within-task transfer; Bugg & Dey, 2018; Bugg & Hutchison, 2013; Bugg et al., 2011; Bustos et al., 2023; Ileri-Tayar et al., 2022).

[PAPER_0028, relevance_score=0.291] In the following transfer phase using the same task, they encountered novel unbiased items (i.e., 50% congruent) that included the predictive cues, intermixed with the biased items. In all three experiments, within-task transfer was found.

[PAPER_0030, relevance_score=0.332] In contrast to within-task transfer, between-task transfer represents a far form of transfer since not only the stimuli but also the overall task goal changes from the training to the transfer phase. However, only one prior study has examined the between-task transfer of learned item-specific control settings to date, to the best of our knowledge (Ileri-Tayar et al., 2022, Experiment 3).

[PAPER_0031, relevance_score=0.305] In that experiment, we investigated transfer of item-specific control to an unbiased novel task (all items were 50% congruent) that included the predictive cues participants associated with control settings in a different task (i.e., the training task). The experiment consisted of two training blocks and one transfer block.

[PAPER_0041, relevance_score=0.302] (2022) by making the following changes to their design: (a) swapping the assignment of training and transfer tasks in Experiment 1, (b) intermixing the tasks in addition to swapping the assignment of training and transfer tasks in Experiment 2, and (c) using a transfer task that did not share the relevant (to-be-named) dimension or response set with the training task to examine a farther version of between-task transfer in Experiment 3.

To further illustrate the research questions of interest in the current study, we offer the following example.

[PAPER_0048, relevance_score=0.284] The novel aspect of the design was the intermixing of the training and transfer trials (tasks) within each block, rather than blocking the tasks in separate phases with transfer following training. Participants switched randomly between the Flanker and the Stroop tasks, performing whichever task was indicated by the stimulus that was presented on a given trial.

[PAPER_0066, relevance_score=0.300] [From Experiment 1, cited for: Design and stimuli, except for intermixed tasks, the more extreme training PC manipulation, and an initial learning phase] These differences between the target and distractor circles were intended to encourage the processing of the distractor dimension, requiring greater control to attend to the target circle.

[PAPER_0071, relevance_score=0.292] [From Experiment 1, cited for: Design and stimuli, except for intermixed tasks, the more extreme training PC manipulation, and an initial learning phase] Stimuli were either congruent (i.e., the color of the shape and the meaning of the word matched) or incongruent (i.e., the color of the shape and the meaning of the word did not match).

[PAPER_0075, relevance_score=0.292] The stimulus organization is presented in Table 3.

The third change from Experiment 1 is that we included a 144-trial learning phase (block) prior to the main experimental phase. The learning phase followed the same design as the experimental phase, intermixing training and transfer items (tasks). The goal of the learning phase before the experimental blocks was to allow participants to learn about the PCs of the predictive cues (colors) before the critical transfer trials.

[PAPER_0090, relevance_score=0.293] Transfer Items (Stroop Task)

We excluded 42 participants from the transfer analysis due to the absence of a positive ISPC effect for the training items. Subsequently, we analyzed the data from the remaining 68 participants.5 We ran a 2 (predictive cue PC: MC vs. MI) × 2 (trial type: congruent vs. incongruent) repeated-measures ANOVA.

[PAPER_0109, relevance_score=0.315] The stimuli looked different, the task goal differed, and there were different conflict types (i.e., a semantic conflict in the Stroop task and a spatial conflict in the Flanker task). Yet, between-task transfer was observed. A potentially critical set of features that did not differ between training and transfer tasks was the relevant (to-be-named) dimension and the response set.

[PAPER_0113, relevance_score=0.290] Regarding generalizability, between-task transfer was observed when the training and transfer task assignments were swapped (i.e., using the Flanker as the training task and the Stroop as the transfer task) in Experiment 1, when the task assignments were swapped and tasks were intermixed (i.e., training and transfer tasks were randomly presented within blocks rather than in separate blocks) in Experiment 2, and when a transfer task (i.e., picture-word Stroop task involving produce naming) that did not share the relevant (to-be-named) dimension or response set with the training task (i.e., color-word Stroop task) was used in an intermixed design representing a farther version of between-task transfer in Experiment 3.

[PAPER_0114, relevance_score=0.279] One notable difference between the patterns of between-task transfer across the three experiments is that uniquely in the last experiment, the between-task transfer effect was limited to the second half of the experiment.

The theoretical implications of these novel findings are four-fold. First, the retrieval and execution of learned control settings in a novel, unbiased task that differs from the task in which they were learned further supports the flexibility and automaticity of learning-guided, item-specific control mechanisms.

[PAPER_0124, relevance_score=0.315] A key decision was to maintain "broad feature similarity" between training and transfer tasks (Cochrane & Pratt, 2022, p. 2). In all experiments, in addition to matching (Experiments 1 and 2) or closely matching (Experiment 3) the color of the predictive cue between tasks, we presented predictive cues as circular (i.e., the shape of the Stroop stimuli and target circle in the Flanker stimuli) or approximately circular shapes (i.e., produce pictures) to create a connection between the training and transfer tasks.

[PAPER_0138, relevance_score=0.283] Participants completed a learning (training) phase in which they experienced a high switch (i.e., sorting rule changed every 10 trials) or a low switch (i.e., sorting rule changed every 30 trials) environment.

Subsequently, they were tested on a transfer phase with a medium switch (i.e., rule changed every 20 trials) environment.

[PAPER_0155, relevance_score=0.287] A continuous approach would depend on using the ISPC effect in training, a difference of differences, to predict the ISPC effect in transfer, also a difference of differences, in a correlational analysis. Such analyses are constrained by the reliability of each of the measures, and given they are both difference of differences scores, this approach does not seem fruitful (Cronbach & Furby, 1970; Lord, 1963; Zimmerman, 2009).

Sample Training and Transfer Items in Ileri-Tayar et al. (2022) and the Current Study

Note. The first two rows of this figure (Experiments 1 and 2 in Ileri-Tayar et al., 2022) demonstrate examples of within-task transfer. The predictive cue (e.g., the color green) repeated across training and transfer items within the same task. While transfer items were presented with the predictive cues from the training items, they were unbiased and presented with novel distractors (i.e., the word purple and the outer circles in purple in these examples).

[PAPER_0172, relevance_score=0.323] The subsequent two rows (Experiment 3 in Ileri-Tayar et al., 2022; Experiments 1 and 2 in the current study) demonstrate examples of between-task transfer. The predictive cue (e.g., the color green) repeated across training and transfer items from different tasks. While transfer items included the predictive cues from the training items, the stimuli and the task were novel and unbiased. The stronger discrepancy across the items results in a far version of transfer compared with the previous two (near transfer) examples.

[PAPER_0173, relevance_score=0.303] The last row (Experiment 3 in the current study) illustrates an even farther version of between-task transfer. While the predictive cue (e.g., the color green) repeated across training and transfer items, the predictive cue was not the relevant dimension for the unbiased transfer items and the response sets were different across tasks. It is the farthest version of between-task transfer we have investigated to date. See Method sections for the detailed description of design and stimuli.
